## Why this unit matters

- Foundations solved SIR to establish theory; this chapter is about the
  **tools** — the `OrdinaryDiffEq` workflow.
- We cover: building an `ODEProblem`, the `Tsit5` solver, dense interpolation
  `sol(t)`, and **callbacks** for events.
- Two events: a time-limited **lockdown** and automatic **peak detection**.

## Equations {.smaller}

Base SIR with a time-dependent, piecewise-constant $\beta(t)$:

$$
\lambda(t)=\frac{\beta(t)\,c\,I}{N},\qquad
\beta(t)=\begin{cases}\beta_\text{lock}, & t_1\le t<t_2,\\ \beta, & \text{else.}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-s-ch03-lockdown}

The infectious peak is the root of the growth rate

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}=\lambda(t)S-\gamma I=0,
$$ {#eq-s-ch03-peak}

which a `ContinuousCallback` locates to solver tolerance.

## Julia API: problem, solver, interpolation

```{julia}
#| label: s-ch03-solve
#| echo: true
using OrdinaryDiffEq
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u; β, c, γ, N = p; λ = β * c * I / N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - γ * I; du[3] = γ * I; return nothing
end
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]; p = (0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000.0); tspan = (0.0, 80.0)
sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
(length(sol.t), round(sol(12.5)[2]; digits = 3))   # adaptive steps; dense interpolant
```

## Julia API: a lockdown & peak detection

```{julia}
#| label: s-ch03-callbacks
#| echo: true
using DiffEqCallbacks
t1, t2 = 10.0, 30.0; β_lock = 0.025
lockdown!(integ) = (integ.p[1] = integ.t < t2 ? β_lock : 0.05)
cb = PresetTimeCallback([t1, t2], lockdown!)
sol_lock = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, [0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000.0]),
                 Tsit5(); callback = cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

peak_t = Float64[]
dIdt(u, p) = p[1] * p[2] * u[2] / p[4] * u[1] - p[3] * u[2]     # eq-s-ch03-peak
peak_cb = ContinuousCallback((u, t, i) -> dIdt(u, i.p), i -> push!(peak_t, i.t))
solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, collect(p)), Tsit5();
      callback = peak_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
(round.(peak_t; digits = 2), round(maximum(sol[2, :]); digits = 1),
 round(maximum(sol_lock[2, :]); digits = 1))
```

## Generated result

```{julia}
#| label: fig-s-ch03-lockdown
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Infectious curve without intervention (red) and with a lockdown halving β over days 10–30 (dashed blue, shaded). The vertical line marks the detected baseline peak."
using CairoMakie
tt = 0.0:0.25:80.0
fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1,1]; xlabel = "day", ylabel = "I(t)", title = "SIR with a lockdown")
vspan!(ax, t1, t2; color = (:grey, 0.15))
lines!(ax, tt, [sol(t)[2] for t in tt];      color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "no intervention")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol_lock(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, linestyle = :dash, label = "lockdown")
vlines!(ax, peak_t; color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "detected peak")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt); fig
```

## Validation

Conservation, interpolation self-consistency, and event-detected peak vs a
brute-force scan:

```{julia}
#| label: s-ch03-check
#| echo: true
cons = all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), 1000.0; atol = 1e-6), sol.u)
interp = isapprox(sol(sol.t[10]), sol.u[10]; atol = 1e-8)
dense_t = 0.0:0.01:80.0
brute = dense_t[argmax([sol(t)[2] for t in dense_t])]
peak_ok = isapprox(peak_t[1], brute; atol = 0.05)
(cons, interp, peak_ok)
```

All `true`: the solver conserves population, its interpolant is faithful, and the
callback peak matches the maximum.

## Limitations & takeaways

- The workflow separates **what** the model is from **how** it is solved and
  **what happens during** the solve — the same `ODEProblem` scales to stiff
  solvers, sensitivity, and fitting.
- Callbacks turn an integrator into an event-driven simulator.
- Limits are those of deterministic SIR; the lockdown here is a perfect switch.
- **Takeaway:** master `ODEProblem` + `Tsit5` + callbacks once, reuse everywhere.

::: {.notes}
Highlight that dense output means sol(t) is a high-order interpolant, not a saved
sample, which is how solutions are resampled onto observation grids later. The
mutable parameter vector is required so the PresetTimeCallback can change β.
Note that realistic interventions involve uncertainty and feedback, deferred to
the interventions and control chapter. Invite learners to sweep β_lock in the
notebook.
:::
